headline: Four AI labs said they'd slow down. Subscribers sued.
summary: Four people who pay for ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini sued Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google in federal court on Friday. They say the companies broke antitrust law by agreeing to slow their AI work, so subscribers get less for their money. The suit points to a Sept. 12 essay by Dario Amodei and same-day agreement from three rival CEOs.

cover_question.q: Is it illegal to be careful?

cover_answer: On your own, no. With your three rivals, that's the suit.
table_question: If the top players all agreed to go easy, is that cheating?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Four companies that make talking computer programs all said they would slow down and be careful. Some customers are suing them. They say four racers can't agree to jog, because everyone watching paid to see a race. A judge will decide, and nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: A five-year-old knows a race and knows jogging. That grown-ups can get in trouble for slowing down is the surprise, and the surprise is enough.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a race is in front of them every recess. The script gives them four runners agreeing to jog and stops there; antitrust can wait ten years. Expect “are they bad?” No. Being careful is fine. The argument is about doing it as a team.

8-12.script: Anthropic's boss wrote that AI labs should slow down together so safety can catch up. OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google agreed that day. Antitrust law bars teaming up to give customers less, so four subscribers sued. A runner may slow down. Fixing the race gets the whistle.
8-12.why: Teaming-up rules are fairness rules, this age's home ground.
8-12.why_long: This age is building chains of cause and effect and testing whether adults apply rules evenly. The script hands them a four-link chain: an essay, three yeses, a law against teaming up, a lawsuit. The referee turns it into a rule they already play by. Expect “but slowing down is good?” It can be. The law asks who agreed, not why.

13-17.script: Should rivals be allowed to agree to slow down if the product might be dangerous? Four AI labs said yes in public, and paying users sued them under antitrust law on Friday. Amodei asked for a government waiver first; Altman said don't wait. Who sets the pace: companies, courts or Congress?
13-17.why: Coordination can protect people and cheat them at once. Let them pick.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: slowing down might keep people safe, and four rivals agreeing to it might cheat the people paying them. The script hands over both and asks who sets the pace. Kuhn's point is that arguing is practised, so take the other side if they pick one. Expect “whose side are you on?” Say, then defend it.

5-7.q: Why are they in trouble for being careful?
5-7.a: Each company can be careful on its own. The customers say the four can't decide it together.

8-12.q: How can slowing down be illegal?
8-12.a: Rivals can't agree to compete less. Slower at the same price is that.

8-12.q: Did they actually make a deal?
8-12.a: One essay, three public yeses on Sept. 12. The companies haven't commented.

13-17.q: Is it illegal to be careful?
13-17.a: Not alone. Agreeing it with three rivals is the deal the suit attacks.

13-17.q: Could AI really kill us all?
13-17.a: Their lawyer says so. The court only asks if the deal cheats subscribers.
